v.why: L2 shrinkage compounds across three layers and attenuates the signal, so extra penalty costs more accuracy in deep nets.
Adam's per-parameter steps change the function more in wide nets, so they hit the divergence cliff sooner.
Many noisy updates per epoch with a larger step cause instability, whereas large batches have few updates and gain from bigger steps.
Deep stacks amplify step-size errors through layers and diverge sooner at larger learning rates.
Averaging more samples tames the gradient noise that makes high learning rates unstable, and lost updates matter less when steps are large.
Narrow nets are capacity- and optimization-limited and benefit from more updates per epoch, while wide nets already fit quickly.
Depth supplies capacity that narrow layers lack.
A single hidden layer relies on width for capacity, while deeper nets already get it from depth.
Wider nets fit faster per update, compensating for the few steps taken with large batches.
Wider nets move further in function space per Adam step, offsetting a tiny learning rate that would otherwise undertrain.
